text: CWE-839: Numeric Range Comparison Without Minimum Check. The product validates that a numeric value is less than or equal to a maximum but omits the corresponding lower-bound check, so negative values pass. The flawed assumption is that the value is inherently non-negative because the UI slider, HTML input, or client SDK prevents negatives. Root causes include maximum-only validation, signed types used for quantities that should be unsigned, and comparisons that treat a negative as trivially satisfying 'less than max'. The defect is invisible to signature-based tooling because the payload is a valid number and the endpoint is legitimate; impact appears when the negative value reaches arithmetic, array indexing, memory operations, or balance updates.

text: CWE-190: Integer Overflow or Wraparound. The product performs arithmetic on a fixed-width integer and assumes the result remains representable, but the operation exceeds the type's range and wraps to a small or negative value. The flawed assumption is that quantities, lengths, counters, prices, or timestamps are bounded by business logic and therefore cannot reach the type limit. Root causes include unchecked multiplication of quantity by size or price, 32-bit counters for unbounded events, signed/unsigned conversions, and length arithmetic performed before allocation. SAST tools may flag some instances, but WAFs cannot detect the pattern because each request is individually valid; the overflow emerges from accumulated state or a single large but accepted value.

text: Business logic flaw: OTP verification is optional rather than mandatory during account signup. The backend creates the account and issues a session whenever the signup payload is otherwise valid, treating the absence of the `code` field as an acceptable state instead of a failed precondition. The flawed assumption is that the client always submits the verification step and that a missing field cannot occur outside the intended UI flow. Root causes include validating the OTP only when present, modeling verification as a client-side step rather than a server-side state transition, and issuing the session before ownership of the email is proven. The request is syntactically valid and uses the legitimate signup endpoint, so WAFs and SAST rules do not flag it; the defect is an absent server-side guard on a required workflow state.

root_causes: OTP comparison skipped when the verification field is absent or null

Verification modeled as a client step instead of server-side pending-registration state

text: Business logic flaw: cashback retailer entitlement is enforced in the mobile UI but not in the merchant-selection API. A non-premium account is limited to three selected retailers, yet the endpoint that updates the selection accepts an arbitrary merchant list, allowing the user to replace the initial three and accrue cashback across every retailer associated with the program. The flawed assumption is that the client's plan-aware UI is the authoritative enforcement point. Root causes include trusting client-supplied merchant identifiers and counts, missing a server-side plan-tier check on update, and treating the initial selection as immutable without enforcing that invariant in the data layer.

root_causes: Merchant list accepted from the client without a server-side plan-tier check
Selection count and merchant eligibility not enforced in the data layer
Plan limits enforced only by the mobile application UI

text: Business logic flaw: the organization's two-factor authentication requirement is enforced when a report is created but not when a collaborator is invited or accepts access. A reporter who has 2FA enabled can invite an account without 2FA, and the invitation is accepted without a step-up check, exposing the same sensitive report the policy was meant to protect. The flawed assumption is that the creator's 2FA status transitively covers every principal who later gains access. Root causes include checking authentication assurance at one workflow entry point, treating collaboration as a metadata operation, and failing to re-evaluate organization policy at access time.

metadata.report_title: Business Logic error leads to bypass 2FA requirement
root_causes: 2FA policy checked at report creation but not at collaboration acceptance
Invitation treated as metadata rather than a privilege grant on a protected object
No re-evaluation of authentication assurance on each access

text: Business logic flaw: product prices are fixed per currency and are not revalued against the current foreign-exchange rate at checkout. The client chooses the billing currency, and the server charges the static local price, so when the currency pair moves the customer can pay materially less than the USD list price. The flawed assumption is that published currency prices remain economically equivalent and that users will not select a currency for arbitrage. Root causes include treating currency as a display preference, storing independent price points without an FX source and timestamp, and failing to recompute the charge from a single base price at payment time.

metadata.title: Static Currency Pricing Enables Foreign-Exchange Arbitrage at Checkout
metadata.report_title: Business Logic, currency arbitrage - Possibility to pay less than the price in USD
root_causes: Independent static price points per currency with no FX source or timestamp
Client-selected currency treated as a display preference rather than a pricing input
Charge amount not recomputed from a single base price at payment time

text: Business logic flaw: the invitation endpoint accepts a client-supplied `access_level` and grants the corresponding role without verifying that the inviter's plan entitles them to assign it. The free plan is supposed to allow only edit access, while read-only access is a Pro feature; the UI hides the option, but the API trusts the request body. Root causes include enforcing plan entitlements only in the frontend, using the request value as the source of truth for role assignment, and failing to validate the role against the inviter's plan at invitation creation and acceptance.

text: Business logic flaw: the password-change flow accepts a new password without verifying the current password and without rejecting reuse of the existing password. Authorization is inferred solely from possession of a valid session, so any request that reaches the endpoint can rotate the credential. The flawed assumption is that an authenticated session proves the actor knows the current password and that users will choose a different value. Root causes include missing re-authentication, no comparison against the stored credential, and no post-change session invalidation. The request is a legitimate authenticated call, so signature-based controls do not flag it.

metadata.report_title: Business logic error
root_causes: Current password not required or verified before rotation

Other sessions and tokens not invalidated after a credential change

text: CWE-20: Improper Input Validation. The product accepts data whose type, range, format, or semantics it never verifies, then routes that data into a business decision such as pricing, entitlement, state change, or resource allocation. This is the parent class of most business-logic bypasses: the request is legitimate in shape, but the value falls outside the contract the downstream logic silently assumes. MITRE classifies this entry as Class with a mapping usage of DISCOURAGED, which means the entry is discouraged as a mapping target because it is too abstract to stand alone. The defect is rarely a single missing check; it is a mismatch between the contract each layer assumes and the data it actually receives. Root causes include validation performed only in the browser, mobile client, or API gateway, checks that confirm syntax but never confirm business meaning or allowed value sets, and validation applied to one representation while a second representation reaches the sink. Because the request is syntactically valid and targets a legitimate business endpoint, signature-based controls and generic SAST rules rarely flag the abuse. The effect becomes observable only when the attacker's action is compared with the intended business invariant and the persisted state.

text: Business logic flaw: the build-save endpoint accepts a custom background identifier and persists it without checking whether the account holds the prime subscription that the cosmetic requires. The restriction exists in the editor interface, which hides premium backgrounds from free members, but the API that saves a build treats the background as ordinary user data. Root causes include entitlement checks performed only in the client, a save handler that trusts the submitted cosmetic identifier, and no server-side reconciliation between the account's plan and the assets stored in the build.

metadata.title: Premium Custom Background Applied Without an Active Subscription
metadata.report_title: Bypass restrict of member subscription to use custom background in https://3d.cs.money without prime subscription
root_causes: Premium cosmetic selection enforced only in the editor interface
Build-save endpoint persisting an arbitrary background identifier
No plan-to-asset reconciliation at save or render time

text: Business logic flaw: the withdrawal-fee endpoint is documented as a user operation and sits beside other private endpoints, but its authentication filter is misconfigured so anonymous requests receive live financial data. Every sibling endpoint rejects unauthenticated calls, which shows that the omission is specific to this route rather than an intentional public API. Root causes include per-route authentication configuration, a route added outside the shared middleware, and a test suite that checks the happy path with a valid signature only.

metadata.title: Private Withdrawal-Fee Endpoint Accessible Without Authentication
metadata.report_title: POST /api/bitcoinWithdrawalFees returns financial data without authentication despite being documented as a USER OPERATION (private endpoint)
root_causes: Authentication middleware omitted from a single private route
Endpoint classification maintained separately from route registration
No negative authentication test for the documented user operations

text: Business logic flaw: the minimum-bounty preference is bounded only by the slider in the interface. The GraphQL mutation accepts any integer, so a researcher can set a threshold above the maximum the product derives from their average payout. The setting then filters private invitations using a value the business never intended to allow, distorting which programs reach the researcher. Root causes include client-side-only bounds, a mutation resolver that validates type but not range, and no server-side derivation of the ceiling.

metadata.title: Invitation Bounty Threshold Bypassed Through a GraphQL Mutation
metadata.report_title: Hacker can bypass minimum bounty amount restrictions in "invitation preferences" setting via UpdateInvitationPreferencesMutation GraphQL operation
root_causes: Range enforced only by the UI slider
GraphQL mutation accepting any integer for the threshold
Ceiling derived in the client instead of the resolver

text: Business logic flaw: the wholesale customer invitation link can be retrieved after the customer has activated their account, even though the product intends the link to be single-use and dead after activation. A staff member whose role covers only apps and channels can invoke the retrieval path and obtain a link that resets the customer's password, resulting in account takeover. Root causes include an invitation state that is not checked on retrieval, a permission model that does not cover the retrieval action, and a link that remains a valid credential after activation.

metadata.title: Activated Customer Invitation Link Recoverable by Limited Staff
metadata.report_title: Staff who only have apps and channels permission can do a takeover account at the wholesale store (Bypass get invitation link)
root_causes: Invitation retrieval not gated by the customer's activation state
Staff role covering a privileged invitation action it should not include
Invitation link still functioning as a password-reset credential

text: Business logic flaw: enabling two-step verification is supposed to require the account password immediately before an OTP device is bound, but the password step can be skipped by calling the enrolment endpoints directly. An attacker who holds a live session, for example on a shared computer, can bind their own phone to the account and then receive every future code. Root causes include a password check implemented only in the wizard, enrolment endpoints that trust session state alone, and no distinction between a normal session and a freshly re-authenticated one.

metadata.title: Two-Factor Enrolment Reached Without Re-Entering the Account Password
metadata.report_title: Bypassed password authentication before enabling OTP verification
root_causes: Password confirmation enforced only in the enrolment wizard
Device-binding endpoints accepting any valid session
No freshness marker for security-sensitive session actions

text: Business logic flaw: the partner portal allows public registration, then treats an account as verified after the applicant uses the password-reset flow on the still-pending account. That sequence bypasses both the email confirmation gate and the SAML requirement, and the activated account can call protected endpoints that return employee names, emails, and profile URLs. Root causes include a reset flow that does not check the account's verification state, activation inferred from any completed flow, and protected endpoints that authorize on account existence rather than on verified membership.

metadata.title: Partner Portal Account Activated by Abusing the Password Reset Flow
metadata.report_title: Unauthenticated Account Registration + Email Verification Bypass + PII Data Leak (2,480 Records) on portal
root_causes: Password reset available and effective for unverified accounts
Verification state not re-checked before protected access
Protected APIs authorizing any active account instead of verified members

text: Business logic flaw: the identity-verification flow accepts documents that do not match the name, date of birth, and address submitted by the applicant, and the same profile fields can later be changed through a personal-information endpoint that the interface does not expose. Verification therefore proves that some identity exists, not that it belongs to this account, and a verified account can be re-pointed to a different person after approval. Root causes include no cross-field consistency check, verification state decoupled from the identity attributes, and an unguarded profile-write endpoint.

metadata.title: KYC Approval With Mismatched Documents and Post-Verification Identity Changes
metadata.report_title: Verification process done using different documents without corresponding to user information / User information can be changed after verification
root_causes: Documents accepted without matching the submitted identity fields
Verification status not bound to the verified attribute values
Profile-write endpoint reachable outside the verified flow

text: Business logic flaw: the OTP logout and login endpoints carry a user_id field that normally equals the caller's own identifier, but the server never verifies that relationship. Substituting the victim's identifier in the logout request causes the OTP flow to operate on the victim's account, and a subsequent login completes as the victim. Root causes include identity taken from the request body, OTP challenges keyed by that supplied identifier, and no binding between the authenticated session and the account being modified.

metadata.title: OTP Logout and Login Accept a Foreign User Identifier
metadata.report_title: Improper Authentication - any user can login as other user with otp/logout & otp/login
root_causes: user_id accepted from the request instead of the session
OTP challenge state keyed by the supplied identifier
No check that the session principal owns the target account

text: Business logic flaw: the invitation endpoint checks the remaining quota and then decrements it in separate steps, so concurrent requests all observe the same balance before any of them writes. Sending many requests at once spends a single invite repeatedly. Cancelling the sent invitations returns them to the balance, which lets the attacker repeat the cycle and generate unlimited invites. Root causes include a non-atomic check-and-decrement, cancellation that credits without reconciling duplicates, and no idempotency key per invitation.

metadata.title: Invitation Quota Overrun Through Concurrent Invitation Requests
metadata.report_title: Race condition in endpoint POST fetlife.com/users/invitation, allow attacker to generate unlimited invites
root_causes: Quota check and decrement performed as separate non-atomic steps
Cancellation crediting invites without deduplicating the original spend
No idempotency key or per-recipient uniqueness constraint

text: Business logic flaw: the mobile profile-activation endpoint verifies a four-digit SMS code, but it neither limits attempts nor expires the code after failures. The attacker with valid credentials submits the full range from 1000 to 9999 and one value is accepted, completing two-factor verification. Root causes include attempt counting performed per session rather than per code, no absolute lifetime for the challenge, and a verification response that does not distinguish a wrong code from a locked challenge.

metadata.title: Four-Digit SMS Code Brute-Forced Without Rate Limit or Expiry
metadata.report_title: Two-factor authentication bypass on Grab Android App
root_causes: No attempt limit on OTP verification
Code does not expire after failed attempts or elapsed time
Challenge state not invalidated when the space is exhausted

text: Business logic flaw: the email-change flow can mark an address as verified without the applicant completing the confirmation sent to that mailbox. The attacker adds an address they do not control, skips the confirmation, and the account is treated as the owner of that address. Private invitations and account-recovery messages for the address are then delivered to the attacker's account context. Root causes include verification state derived from an unrelated action, a confirmation step that is optional, and address ownership inferred from the account that submitted it.

metadata.title: Email Address Verified Without Receiving the Confirmation Message
metadata.report_title: Email Verification Bypass And Get access to user's private invitation.
root_causes: Verification state set by an unrelated completed action
Confirmation step optional in the change flow
Address ownership inferred from the submitting account

text: Business logic flaw: the authentication gateway keys its rate limit on the X-Forwarded-For header, which the client can set. Sending a different address on each request resets the counter, so the attacker can attempt logins, enumerate accounts, and guess OTPs without effective throttling. Root causes include trust in a forwarding header that is not stripped at the edge, a throttle keyed on a spoofable value, and no independent per-account limit.

metadata.title: Login Rate Limit Keyed on a Client-Controlled Forwarded Address
metadata.report_title: Rate limit bypass on passport.acronis.work using X-Forwarded-For request header
root_causes: X-Forwarded-For trusted without a pinned proxy chain
Rate limit keyed only on the client-supplied address
No per-account or per-credential throttle

text: Business logic flaw: the account-recovery setup accepts a phone number and saves it as the recovery channel without verifying the SMS OTP sent to that number. The attacker adds the victim's number to their own account, and subsequent two-factor codes for that number are delivered to the victim while the attacker's account treats the channel as trusted. The same gap lets an attacker bind a number they do not control and manipulate recovery for the account. Root causes include a verification step that is not enforced before persistence, recovery state that trusts an unverified channel, and no re-check when the channel is used for authentication.

metadata.title: Account-Recovery Phone Number Stored Without OTP Verification
metadata.report_title: Bypassing the victim's phone number OTP in the account recovery process on HackerOne
root_causes: Recovery number persisted before OTP verification
Recovery flow treating an unverified channel as trusted
No binding check when the channel is later used for codes

text: Business logic flaw: the credential-update mutation replaces the TOTP secret and regenerates backup codes while requiring only the account password and a code from the new secret, not a code from the existing factor. An attacker who knows the password can enroll their own authenticator and lock the legitimate user out. Root causes include verification against the new secret instead of the old one, backup-code regeneration without step-up authentication, and no notification or delay before the old factor is replaced.

metadata.title: Two-Factor Secret and Backup Codes Replaced Without the Current OTP
metadata.report_title: Changing the 2FA secret key and backup codes without knowing the 2FA OTP
root_causes: New secret accepted as proof instead of the existing factor
Credential-update mutation missing current-OTP verification
Backup codes regenerated without step-up or notification

text: Business logic flaw: the payment billing-edit page and its submit handler are reachable using only the payment identifier in the URL. Neither authentication nor ownership is checked, so an anonymous visitor who obtains a payment UUID can open the form and rewrite the customer's name, address, and billing details. Root causes include object access keyed solely on an identifier, a route outside the authenticated area, and no re-authentication or audit event for financial-data changes.

metadata.title: Payment Billing Information Editable Without Authentication
metadata.report_title: Unauthenticated IDOR allows modification of payment customer billing information
root_causes: Payment edit route keyed only on the object identifier
No authentication or ownership check on the handler
Financial-data change without step-up or audit trail

text: Business logic flaw: leaving a private program through the fast-tracked flow promises an automated invitation elsewhere, and the security@ forwarding feature generates invitations from inbound mail. The two features combined let a researcher cycle out of a program, collect a new private invite, and repeat, harvesting invitations broadly. Root causes include an incentive that issues new entitlements without deduplicating what the researcher already received, eligibility not re-checked at issuance, and no cap on invitation churn.

metadata.title: Private Program Invitations Harvested Through the Leave-Program Reward
metadata.report_title: Harvesting all private invites using leave program fast-tracked invitation and security email forwarding feature
root_causes: Leave-program reward issuing a new invite without deduplication
Eligibility not re-verified at invitation issuance
No cap or cooldown on invitation churn

text: Business logic flaw: a client-visible debug or information-disclosure surface reveals values that the two-factor flow accepts as proof, so an attacker with only a hijacked session can bypass 2FA and then perform post-compromise actions such as changing the email or disabling the factor. The underlying design assumes the attacker lacks a specific secret, but that secret is exposed by the application itself. Root causes include sensitive diagnostics in production, 2FA decisions based on a value the client can read, and post-compromise actions that do not require a fresh factor.

metadata.title: Debug Disclosure Enables Two-Factor Bypass and Post-Compromise Actions
metadata.report_title: Information disclosure -> 2fa bypass -> POST exploitation
root_causes: Sensitive values exposed in debug or diagnostic responses
2FA acceptance of a client-readable value as proof
Post-compromise actions allowed without fresh factor verification

text: Business logic flaw: the login flow decides whether 2FA succeeded by reading a flag in a response that the client can modify, instead of requiring the server to establish an authenticated session only after verifying the code. The attacker with valid credentials intercepts the failed verification response, changes the flag, and the browser proceeds to the authenticated area. Root causes include client-side enforcement of the 2FA outcome, a session issued before verification completes, and no server-side re-check on subsequent requests.

metadata.title: Login Flow Trusts a Client-Modified 2FA Success Response
metadata.report_title: 2FA Bypass via Response Manipulation on Login Page
root_causes: 2FA outcome enforced by a client-modifiable response flag
Authenticated session issued before code verification
Subsequent requests not checked for completed verification

text: Business logic flaw: the checkout router page is intended to be shown once, immediately after payment, and is addressed by a checkout identifier derived from a basket key. The page can be reopened by crafting that key, and the identifiers are guessable enough to enumerate. Each hit reveals another buyer's items, prices, name, billing address, email, and phone number. Root causes include a confirmation page keyed only on a client-supplied identifier, no session or order-ownership check, and low-entropy identifiers with no rate limit.

metadata.title: One-Time Checkout Router Reopened by Brute-Forcing the Basket Key
metadata.report_title: Bypassing one-time checkout router page (revealing payment information)
root_causes: Confirmation page keyed only on a client-supplied checkout key
No session or order-ownership validation
Low-entropy identifiers without rate limiting

text: Business logic flaw: a device is marked trusted for one month after the attacker's own OTP verification, and that trust survives an email change to an address belonging to a victim who has not registered. The attacker keeps a session associated with the victim's email without ever completing 2FA for it, and the real owner only regains control after a password reset. Root causes include device trust scoped to the device rather than the verified identity, an email change that does not invalidate trust, and no re-verification when the account identifier changes.

metadata.title: Email Change Reuses a Trusted-Device Session and Bypasses 2FA
metadata.report_title: 2FA Bypass leads to impersonation of legitimate users
root_causes: Device trust scoped to the device instead of the verified identity
Email change not invalidating trusted-device state
No re-verification when the account identifier changes

text: Business logic flaw: every job vacancy is supposed to be reviewed by an administrator before publication, but the GraphQL mutation that updates a vacancy's status accepts a client-supplied status and applies it without checking that the review actually happened. The attacker publishes arbitrary content directly, bypassing the moderation that protects candidates from spam and phishing. Root causes include a status field writable by the content owner, no separation between requested and approved states, and a moderation check implemented only in the review interface.

metadata.title: Job Vacancy Published Without the Required Admin Approval
metadata.report_title: inDriver Job - Admin Approval Bypass
root_causes: Publication status writable by the vacancy owner
No distinction between requested and approved states
Moderation enforced only in the admin interface

text: Business logic flaw: the points plugin assumes that the processing order status means the order has been paid. Cash-on-delivery orders move to processing immediately, so points are credited before any money is collected and are instantly spendable. The attacker orders repeatedly, earns points, spends them, and abandons or cancels payment. Root causes include accrual keyed on a status that does not prove settlement, no reversal when an order is cancelled or refunded, and points becoming spendable before a settlement event.

metadata.title: Loyalty Points Credited on Cash-on-Delivery Orders Before Payment
metadata.report_title: Gaining unlimited bonus points on websites with WooCommerce Points and Rewards
root_causes: Accrual triggered by processing status rather than payment settlement
No points reversal on cancellation, refund, or failed delivery
Points spendable before settlement confirms

text: Business logic flaw: the billing page is hidden from members in the navigation, but the route itself does not check for the billing-administrator role. A member who enters the URL directly sees payment methods and can begin adding a new one. Root causes include access control implemented as menu visibility, a route registered outside the billing permission check, and no server-side role test on the page or its actions.

metadata.title: Member Role Can Open the Hidden Billing and Payment Page
metadata.report_title: A member-member privilege could access the billing payment page even though the billing page is hidden from the menu
root_causes: Menu visibility used as the access control
Billing route missing the role check
Payment actions not independently authorized

text: Business logic flaw: the public subscription endpoint accepts unlimited requests. The only protection is a transient 429 that can be avoided by pacing requests, so an attacker can subscribe arbitrary addresses, generate mailbombs, damage sender reputation, and enumerate which addresses are already subscribed. Root causes include a throttle that limits concurrency rather than volume, no per-address verification, and no distinction between the first request and repeated requests for the same address.

metadata.title: Email Subscription Endpoint Lacks Effective Throttling
metadata.report_title: No rate limit in email subscription
root_causes: Throttle limits burst rate but not total volume
No per-address confirmation or cooldown
Response differences enable address enumeration

text: Business logic flaw: setting up two-factor authentication requires confirming the account email with a six-digit code, but the confirmation endpoint does not limit attempts. The attacker guesses the code, verifies the victim's email from their own session, and then binds their phone as the second factor, locking the victim out. Root causes include no attempt counter on the email confirmation, a code that remains valid across many failures, and enrolment proceeding from a weakly proven email state.

metadata.title: Six-Digit Email Confirmation Code Brute-Forced During 2FA Setup
metadata.report_title: Email Verification Bypass by bruteforcing when setting up 2FA
root_causes: No attempt limit on email confirmation
Code valid across unlimited failures
Enrolment trusting a weakly proven email state

text: Business logic flaw: the 2FA linking endpoint accepts a user ID from the request, so an attacker can start linking a factor to any account whose ID is known. The verification endpoint then accepts a valid code for that ID without requiring the account's password or session. An account that never enabled 2FA can therefore be taken over by linking the attacker's device and logging in with it. Root causes include identity supplied by the client, verification decoupled from primary authentication, and no check that the account owner consented to the link.

metadata.title: Two-Factor Linking Bound to a Supplied User ID and Verifiable Without Credentials
metadata.report_title: Account takeover w/o interaction for a user that doesn't have 2fa enabled via 2fa linking and improper auth at /api/2fa/verify
root_causes: User ID accepted from the request during factor linking
Verification endpoint not requiring primary authentication
No ownership or consent check before binding a factor

text: Business logic flaw: the authentication service accepts repeated MFA code attempts without an effective limit, so an attacker with the victim's email and password can sweep a numeric range around plausible codes until one is accepted. The transition from 303 to 302 marks success. Root causes include no per-challenge attempt budget, a code that remains valid during the sweep, and no lockout or alert after abnormal volume.

metadata.title: MFA Token Brute-Forceable on the Authentication Service
metadata.report_title: 2FA bypass possible on https://authsvc.singlestore.com
root_causes: No attempt budget per MFA challenge
Code valid for the duration of the sweep
No anomaly detection or lockout on volume

text: Business logic flaw: the customer promotion endpoint accepts a bearer token and a promo code and reports whether the pair is valid, but it applies no multifactor check, no blacklist after failures, and no rate limit. An attacker enumerates tokens at line speed until a valid pair is found, then applies promotions to accounts they do not own. Root causes include a low-assurance endpoint for a value-bearing action, unlimited guessing, and a response that distinguishes valid from invalid tokens.

metadata.title: Promo Endpoint Allows Unlimited Token Enumeration Without MFA or Throttling
metadata.report_title: The Uber Promo Customer Endpoint Does Not Implement Multifactor Authentication, Blacklisting or Rate Limiting
root_causes: Promotion action reachable with a bearer token alone
No rate limit, blacklist, or lockout after failures
Response distinguishes valid tokens from invalid ones

text: Business logic flaw: a program can require two-factor authentication and can blacklist a reporter, but those rules are enforced only on the main submission path. The embedded submission form creates reports through a different channel that skips the requirement and the blacklist. Root causes include policy enforcement duplicated per channel, an embedded flow that creates reports without consulting program eligibility, and no shared pre-submission gate.

metadata.title: Program Submission Requirements Bypassed Through the Embedded Form
metadata.report_title: Hacker can bypass 2FA requirement and reporter blacklist through embedded submission form
root_causes: Eligibility rules enforced per submission channel
Embedded form creating reports without a policy check
No shared pre-submission gate

text: Business logic flaw: the signup provisioning endpoint takes the account identity from an EmailAddress parameter in the request rather than from the verified registration session. By changing the parameter to an existing or victim address, the attacker provisions or activates an account for that address without controlling its mailbox. Root causes include identity taken from a mutable request field, the verification step evaluating a different value than the one provisioned, and no binding between the signup session and the created account.

metadata.title: Signup Provisioning Accepts an Arbitrary EmailAddress Parameter
metadata.report_title: Email verification bypass via request to endpoint accounts.insightly.com/signup/provisionuser
root_causes: Account identity taken from a mutable EmailAddress parameter
Verification evaluating a different value than provisioning
No binding between the signup session and the created account

text: Business logic flaw: the workspace enforces a hard limit of ten folders per space by counting existing folders before creating a new one. After deleting a folder, the attacker sends many creation requests simultaneously; all of them observe nine folders and all are accepted, producing more than ten. Root causes include a non-atomic count-and-create, no unique constraint or quota row, and delete freeing capacity without serializing concurrent creates.

metadata.title: Folder Quota Exceeded Through Concurrent Creation Requests
metadata.report_title: Race Condition in Folder Creation Allows Bypassing Folder Limit
root_causes: Count-and-create performed as separate non-atomic steps
No transactional quota row or constraint
Delete freeing capacity without serializing creates

text: Business logic flaw: an administrator can invite another administrator, but removing the inviter does not invalidate the pending invitation. The invited party can still accept and receive admin privileges after the inviter has been removed from the team, and an already accepted invitee remains an administrator. Root causes include invitations treated as independent grants, no cascade on inviter revocation, and accepted membership not linked to the authority that created it.

metadata.title: Pending Admin Invitations Survive Removal of the Inviting Administrator
metadata.report_title: Pending invites remain valid even after the inviter is removed.
root_causes: Pending invitations independent of the inviter's current authority
No cascade when the inviter is removed
Accepted membership not linked to its granting authority

text: Business logic flaw: the bulk purchase endpoint accepts per-item quantities and computes the order total by summing price times quantity. Negative quantities are not rejected, so an attacker adds a negative line item that subtracts from the total while the positive items are still delivered. Root causes include no sign validation on quantity, totals computed from client-supplied values, and no reconciliation against the catalogue price at authorization time.

metadata.title: Negative Line-Item Quantity Reduces the Marketplace Order Total
metadata.report_title: An attacker can buy marketplace articles for lower prices as it allows for negative quantity values
root_causes: No non-negative validation on quantity
Order total computed from client-supplied line values
No catalogue-price reconciliation before charge

text: Business logic flaw: some private programs restrict participation by locality or jurisdiction, but the invitation system selects researchers by reputation and sends automated invites without evaluating those rules. An ineligible researcher receives and accepts the invitation, and the program's compliance boundary is broken. Root causes include eligibility rules stored as program text rather than structured policy, invitation generation that ignores jurisdiction, and no check at acceptance time.

metadata.title: Private Program Invitations Issued Without Checking Jurisdiction Rules
metadata.report_title: Proper verification is not done before sending invitations to researchers for certain private programs with rules e.g. Participants must be US-based
root_causes: Eligibility rules stored as free text rather than structured policy
Invitation generation based only on reputation
No eligibility check at acceptance

text: Business logic flaw: the tenant can deny invitations to specific email domains, but the comparison uses the raw string. Replacing the letter i in the denied domain with the Unicode character İ produces a string that does not match the denylist yet is delivered to the same mailbox after normalization. Root causes include domain comparison on unnormalized input, no IDNA or case folding before matching, and invitation delivery accepting a broader set of addresses than the policy checks.

metadata.title: Denied Email Domain Bypassed with a Unicode Dotless I Character
metadata.report_title: Bypassing the block of Security Domain Restriction and normally invite blocked domains with special characters
root_causes: Denylist comparison on unnormalized domain strings
No IDNA or Unicode case folding before matching
Invitation delivery accepting addresses the policy rejects

text: Business logic flaw: live-chat transcripts are stored as static text files named with an incrementing number, and the retrieval endpoint serves any file the caller names. There is no check that the transcript belongs to the requesting user, so changing the filename exposes other conversations. In the lab the leaked transcript contains a password that enables account takeover. Root causes include direct object references in a URL, authorization based on knowing the filename, and predictable identifiers.

metadata.title: Chat Transcript Files Addressable by Incrementing Filename
metadata.lab_title: Insecure direct object references
root_causes: Transcript files served directly by predictable filename
No ownership check on the retrieval endpoint
Sensitive content stored in a broadly reachable static location

text: Business logic flaw: the admin role-change endpoint applies its access control based on the HTTP method. The administrative interface uses POST, and the server treats POST as the privileged path without checking the caller's role. A non-admin who replays the same POST with their own session is allowed to promote an account. Root causes include authorization derived from method semantics, a shared handler for privileged and unprivileged callers, and no role check inside the promotion logic.

metadata.title: Role-Promotion Endpoint Authorized by HTTP Method Rather Than Role
metadata.lab_title: Method-based access control can be circumvented
root_causes: Authorization decision derived from the HTTP method
Shared handler for admin and non-admin callers
No role check inside the promotion operation

text: Business logic flaw: changing a user's role is a two-step process, and the second confirmation step does not check the caller's role. The first step is properly protected, but an attacker can invoke the confirmation directly with a non-admin session and complete the promotion. Root causes include authorization applied to the entry point instead of every transition, workflow state that can be manufactured by the client, and no re-validation of the original request.

metadata.title: Role-Change Confirmation Step Missing an Access Control Check
metadata.lab_title: Multi-step process with no access control on one step
root_causes: Authorization enforced only on the first workflow step
Confirmation state constructible by the client
No re-validation of the original promotion request

text: Business logic flaw: the role-change endpoint decides whether a request came from the admin panel by reading the Referer header. Any caller can set that header, so a non-admin who copies the admin panel URL into a promotion request is treated as authorized. Root causes include authorization based on a client-controlled header, no role check on the endpoint, and confusion between origin evidence and entitlement.

metadata.title: Admin Role Change Trusts the Referer Header as Proof of Origin
metadata.lab_title: Referer-based access control
root_causes: Referer header used as an authorization signal
No server-side role check on the promotion endpoint
Origin evidence confused with entitlement

text: Business logic flaw: the administrative panel is not protected by any authentication or role check. Its path is disclosed in robots.txt, so an unauthenticated visitor can open it and use its actions. Root causes include reliance on the panel being unlinked, disclosure of the path in a public file, and no server-side authorization on the route or its actions.

metadata.title: Administrative Panel Reachable Without Any Authorization
metadata.lab_title: Unprotected admin functionality
root_causes: No authentication or role check on the admin route
Admin path disclosed in robots.txt
Reliance on the panel being unlinked

text: Business logic flaw: the admin panel is placed at an unpredictable path and treated as protected because the path is hard to guess. The path is embedded in client-side JavaScript that conditionally renders an admin link, so anyone who reads the script learns it. Root causes include security through obscurity, no server-side role check on the panel, and disclosure of the path in a public asset.

metadata.title: Admin Panel Protected Only by an Obscure URL Disclosed in Client Script
metadata.lab_title: Unprotected admin functionality with unpredictable URL
root_causes: Obscure URL treated as the access control
Admin path embedded in client JavaScript
No server-side role check on the panel

text: Business logic flaw: a front-end system blocks external access to /admin, but the backend framework honors the X-Original-URL header and routes requests based on it. Sending a harmless public path in the request line and the admin path in the header reaches the panel, which has no authentication of its own. Root causes include path-based blocking at the edge, backend trust in a routing header, and no role check on the panel.

metadata.title: Front-End Path Block Bypassed with the X-Original-URL Header
metadata.lab_title: URL-based access control can be circumvented
root_causes: Access control implemented by blocking a path at the front end
Backend trusting X-Original-URL for routing
No authentication on the admin panel itself

text: Business logic flaw: the account page selects the user by an id parameter in the URL instead of the authenticated session. Changing id to another username returns that user's profile, including the API key. Root causes include object identity taken from the request, no ownership check on the profile query, and sensitive credentials rendered on a page that accepts an arbitrary identifier.

metadata.title: Account Page Loads the User Named in the id Parameter
metadata.lab_title: User ID controlled by request parameter
root_causes: Profile selected by a client-supplied id parameter
No ownership check on the profile query
API key rendered on a parameterized page

text: Business logic flaw: the account page still loads the user named in the id parameter, but when the identifier does not match the session it redirects to the home page. The redirect response body is not cleared and still contains the loaded profile, including the API key. Root causes include load-then-check ordering, denial implemented as a redirect without discarding the response body, and credentials included in the page model.

metadata.title: Redirect Response Body Leaks the Requested User's API Key
metadata.lab_title: User ID controlled by request parameter with data leakage in redirect
root_causes: Profile loaded before the ownership check
Redirect issued without clearing the response body
API key included in the page model

text: Business logic flaw: the account page renders the current user's existing password in a masked input, and the user is selected by an id parameter. Changing id to administrator returns the administrator's password in the page source, which the attacker uses to log in and perform administrative actions. Root causes include reversible password storage or decryption for display, identity taken from the request, and no separation between profile data and credentials.

metadata.title: Account Page Prefills the Password of Any Requested User
metadata.lab_title: User ID controlled by request parameter with password disclosure
root_causes: Password rendered to the client in a prefilled field
Identity taken from the request parameter
No separation between profile data and credentials

text: Business logic flaw: the account page selects the user by a GUID, which makes identifiers hard to guess but does not make them authorization. The GUID of another user is disclosed in a public blog author link, so the attacker substitutes it and reads that user's API key. Root causes include treating an unguessable identifier as an access control, no ownership check on the profile query, and disclosure of user GUIDs in public content.

metadata.title: Profile Lookup Uses a GUID That Is Disclosed Elsewhere in the Application
metadata.lab_title: User ID controlled by request parameter, with unpredictable user IDs
root_causes: Unguessable identifier treated as authorization
No ownership check on the profile query
User GUIDs disclosed in public content

text: Business logic flaw: the profile update response includes the user's roleid, and the update handler binds any roleid supplied in the request. A normal user who adds roleid=2 to the email-change request promotes themselves and gains access to the admin panel. Root causes include the persistence model bound directly to the request, role exposed in a profile response, and no field allowlist on the update.

metadata.title: Profile Update Binds a Client-Supplied roleid into the User Record
metadata.lab_title: User role can be modified in user profile
root_causes: Profile update bound to the full user model
Role identifier exposed in the profile response
No allowlist on writable profile fields

text: Business logic flaw: the application identifies administrators by a cookie named Admin whose value is a plain boolean. Any user can set it to true and the server treats them as an administrator, exposing the admin panel and its destructive actions. Root causes include role stored in client-controlled state, no signature or server-side lookup for the cookie, and administrative routes that trust the cookie alone.

metadata.title: Administrative Access Decided by an Unsigned Admin Cookie
metadata.lab_title: User role controlled by request parameter
root_causes: Role stored in an unsigned client cookie
No server-side lookup of the role on each request
Administrative routes trusting the cookie value

text: Business logic flaw: the application publishes interactive API documentation that enumerates its endpoints, methods, and parameters. The documented user endpoint accepts an arbitrary username and deletes the record, and its authorization is limited to 'is authenticated' rather than 'may administer users'. The documentation turns discovery into a checklist, so an ordinary account deletes another user without any guessing. Root causes include documentation left reachable in production, a destructive operation guarded only by authentication, and no object-level check on the username parameter.

metadata.title: Interactive API Documentation Exposes User Deletion to Any Authenticated Caller
metadata.lab_title: Exploiting an API endpoint using documentation
root_causes: Interactive API documentation reachable in production
Destructive endpoint guarded by authentication only
No ownership or role check on the username parameter

text: Business logic flaw: the checkout endpoint accepts an order object and binds it to the order model, which includes a chosen_discount field that the interface never sends. Because the binder persists any field present in the request, an ordinary shopper adds a discount identifier and buys a high-value item at a reduced total. Root causes include the request model being the persistence model, a discount field that is readable in the checkout response, and no allowlist on writable order fields.

metadata.title: Checkout Binds a Hidden chosen_discount Field into the Order
metadata.lab_title: Exploiting a mass assignment vulnerability
root_causes: Checkout request bound directly to the persistence model
Discount field exposed in the checkout GET response
No allowlist separating client-settable from server-derived fields

text: Business logic flaw: the product page fetches prices from a read-only API route that the interface only ever calls with GET. The same route also implements PATCH, which updates the stored price with no role check and no validation that the caller should be able to price an item. Changing the method turns a read path into a write path that rewrites the basket total. Root causes include unreferenced write methods left registered on a public route, no method allowlist per route, and pricing data writable by any authenticated shopper.

metadata.title: Price Endpoint Accepts PATCH on a Route the Interface Only Reads
metadata.lab_title: Exploiting an unused API endpoint
root_causes: Unused PATCH handler registered on the public price route
No per-route method allowlist
Price writable by an ordinary shopper

text: Business logic flaw: the forgot-password handler forwards the submitted username into a server-side request to an internal API without encoding it. Injecting an encoded ampersand adds parameters to that internal query, and a fragment truncates the rest of it. The attacker manipulates the internal lookup and, combined with the reset flow, obtains control of the administrator account. Root causes include string-concatenated URLs, no allowlist for forwarded parameters, and an internal API that trusts parameters the front end never intended to expose.

metadata.title: Password Reset Forwards an Unescaped Parameter into an Internal Query String
metadata.lab_title: Exploiting server-side parameter pollution in a query string
root_causes: Username concatenated into an internal query string without encoding
Internal API accepts arbitrary additional parameters
No validation of the composed request before dispatch

text: Business logic flaw: the password reset handler places the submitted username into a REST path segment of an internal request. Because the value is not encoded, traversal sequences move the request from the user resource into the administrative resource, and API documentation discovered separately supplies a field the internal endpoint accepts. The attacker exploits the composed path to reset the administrator's password. Root causes include unencoded path concatenation, a broad internal API surface, and no per-segment validation.

metadata.title: REST Path Segment Built from User Input Allows Path Traversal into Admin Routes
metadata.lab_title: Exploiting server-side parameter pollution in a REST URL
root_causes: Username concatenated into a REST path without encoding
Traversal sequences not rejected in a path segment
Internal admin API reachable from the public lookup route

text: Business logic flaw: the second login step accepts a verify parameter that names whose code is being checked, and the server uses that value instead of the session principal. The attacker logs in with their own credentials, changes verify to the victim's username, and the challenge becomes the victim's. Combined with an attempt limit that is per session rather than per code, the attacker brute-forces the victim's code from their own session. Root causes include identity taken from the request, challenge state keyed by that identifier, and attempt counting that resets with each new login.

metadata.title: Second-Factor Verification Trusts a Client-Supplied verify Parameter
metadata.lab_title: 2FA broken logic
root_causes: verify parameter trusted as the challenge identity
Challenge state keyed by the client-supplied identifier
Attempt limit scoped per session instead of per challenge

text: Business logic flaw: the login flow completes the first factor and then presents a second-factor page, but the session issued at that point is already sufficient to reach protected pages. The 2FA step is a navigation gate, not a server-side authorization requirement. Anyone holding a valid password can skip the prompt by requesting the account page directly. Root causes include a full session issued before verification, protected routes that check only authentication, and no verified flag evaluated server-side.

metadata.title: Authenticated Area Reachable by Navigating Past the 2FA Prompt
metadata.lab_title: 2FA simple bypass
root_causes: Full session issued before the second factor is verified
Protected routes checking authentication only
No server-side verified marker on the session

text: Business logic flaw: the second-factor form accepts a four-digit code and permits repeated attempts. The only obstacle is that the challenge rotates, which an attacker handles by re-requesting the login page and resubmitting within the same session using an automated macro. The code space is then swept until one value is accepted. Root causes include no per-challenge attempt budget, a code short enough to enumerate, and no lockout or alert on abnormal volume.

metadata.title: Four-Digit 2FA Code Accepts Repeated Attempts with No Effective Limit
metadata.lab_title: 2FA bypass using a brute-force attack
root_causes: No attempt limit per challenge or per account
Four-digit code space small enough to enumerate
No lockout or alert on repeated failures

text: Business logic flaw: the reset confirmation form submits both a token and a username, and the handler uses the username to select the account while treating the token as a formality. A token issued to the attacker's own account is therefore accepted for the victim's account, and the new password is applied to the victim. Root causes include identity taken from the request at confirmation time, token validation not bound to the account, and tokens that are not single-use.

metadata.title: Reset Confirmation Trusts the Submitted Username Instead of the Token
metadata.lab_title: Password reset broken logic
root_causes: Username taken from the confirmation request
Token not bound to the account it was issued for
Token validity checked without consumption

text: Business logic flaw: the password reset email builds its link from the request host, which can be overridden with X-Forwarded-Host. The attacker requests a reset for the victim while setting that header to their own domain, and the victim receives a genuine reset email pointing at the attacker's server. When the victim clicks, the token is captured and the attacker resets the password. Root causes include host taken from a client-controllable header, no allowlist of canonical hosts, and tokens usable from any requester.

metadata.title: Reset Link Host Taken from a Client-Controlled Forwarded Header
metadata.lab_title: Password reset poisoning via middleware
root_causes: Reset link host derived from a client-controllable header
No canonical host allowlist for generated links
Captured token usable by any requester

text: Business logic flaw: the change-password form includes the username as a hidden field, and the handler uses it to select the account while validating the current password. Two behaviours combine into an oracle: a wrong current password returns an error naming the username, while a correct one succeeds. The attacker submits the victim's username with candidate passwords, and because the form is authenticated with the attacker's own session, throttling does not apply. Root causes include identity taken from the request, response differences that reveal credential validity, and no session binding.

metadata.title: Password Change Form Accepts a Username and Leaks the Current Password by Response
metadata.lab_title: Password brute-force via password change
root_causes: Username taken from a hidden form field
Response differing between wrong password and success
No session binding or throttle on password change

text: Business logic flaw: the login endpoint accepts JSON and binds the password field without enforcing that it is a single string. Submitting an array of candidate passwords makes the server evaluate each value while the rate limiter counts the request as one attempt. The attacker tries the entire candidate list in a single call and identifies success by which password the session ends up using. Root causes include a weak type constraint in the request parser, throttling counted per request rather than per credential test, and no rejection of multi-value fields.

metadata.title: Login Accepts an Array of Passwords in a Single JSON Request
metadata.lab_title: Broken brute-force protection, multiple credentials per request
root_causes: Password field accepts an array instead of a single string
Throttle counted per request rather than per credential
No schema validation rejecting multi-value credentials

text: Business logic flaw: the login endpoint blocks an IP after a fixed number of consecutive failures, but a successful login resets the counter. Because the attacker owns a valid account, they can interleave their own successful authentication between candidate attempts for the victim, keeping the counter low while still testing many passwords. Root causes include a failure counter scoped to the IP rather than the target account, reset on any success rather than per account, and no distributed or per-account limit.

metadata.title: Per-IP Failure Counter Reset by Interleaving a Successful Login
metadata.lab_title: Broken brute-force protection, IP block
root_causes: Failure counter scoped to the source IP only
Counter reset by any successful login, including another account
No per-account attempt budget
